title: CEO Interview with Jerry Chen of Upbeat Technology - Semiwiki
gist: Taiwan-based Upbeat Technology (founded 2017, >$20M raised since 2021, Tier 1 US and Japan design wins by 2023) pairs MEMS bone-conduction/vibration sensors with ultra-low-power RISC-V AI SoCs using compute-in-memory and near-threshold computing. CEO Jerry Chen's differentiating claim is treating sensing and inference as one system problem, with the strongest current pull from drone controllers and dexterous-hand tactile sensing in robotics rather than consumer wearables.

themes.theme: Sensing plus compute as one architecture

insights.claim: Upbeat Technology's core differentiation claim is that many companies offer sensors and others offer AI processors, but very few develop both with a common architecture designed specifically for always-on intelligence.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Sensor-plus-inference co-design is the emerging competitive axis in edge AI silicon; pure-play MEMS vendors and pure-play NPU IP vendors are both exposed to it.
insights.quote: Many companies offer sensors. Others offer AI processors. Very few develop both technologies with a common architecture designed specifically for always-on intelligence.
insights.locator: What does the competitive landscape look like

insights.claim: Upbeat treats sensing and intelligence as a single system challenge rather than two separate components, which lets it optimize a customer's entire system architecture instead of supplying a discrete component.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: System-level engagement raises switching costs and ASP per design win versus component sales — the metric to test in any edge-AI startup diligence.
insights.quote: we view sensing and intelligence as a single system challenge rather than two separate components

insights.claim: The stated founding thesis is that the future of edge AI depends on dramatically improving both sensing and power efficiency simultaneously — conventional sensors fail to capture rich enough data for advanced AI while conventional architectures burn too much power for always-on operation.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Frames edge AI's bottleneck as a two-sided data-quality-plus-power problem, not just a TOPS/watt race.
insights.quote: the future of edge AI depends on dramatically improving both sensing and power efficiency

insights.claim: Customers of edge-AI silicon are balancing three competing priorities — performance, power consumption and product cost — and many discover that adding AI functionality creates power and thermal challenges that limit product viability.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Thermal/power failure at the product level, not model accuracy, is what kills consumer edge-AI devices — a screening question for any AI hardware roadmap.
insights.quote: Many companies discover that adding AI functionality quickly creates power and thermal challenges that limit product viability.
insights.locator: What keeps your customers up at night?

insights.claim: Upbeat's ultra-low-power AI SoCs are built around advanced RISC-V architectures with integrated AI acceleration, DSP functionality, compute-in-memory and near-threshold computing techniques.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: A concrete example of RISC-V displacing Arm in always-on, power-constrained sensor hubs — the segment where RISC-V share gains are most credible.

insights.claim: Upbeat is exploring compute-in-memory as a next-generation approach to further cut power for complex neural network computations and enable new classes of always-on intelligent systems.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Compute-in-memory commercialization at the microwatt edge is likely to arrive before it does in datacenter — watch the low-power segment for first proof points.
insights.locator: We are also exploring next-generation approaches

insights.claim: Local on-device AI processing without constant cloud connectivity delivers four distinct commercial benefits — longer operating life, faster response, improved privacy and reduced cloud dependence — bundling privacy and cost arguments alongside the technical one.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: The privacy and cloud-cost arguments are what let edge inference win budget even when cloud inference is technically adequate.
insights.quote: operate longer, respond faster, improve privacy, and reduce dependence on cloud resources

themes.theme: Robotics tactile sensing as the pull market

insights.claim: Upbeat reports its strongest momentum in drones and robotics — specifically dexterous hand tactile sensing, where miniature high-sensitivity vibration sensors let robots perceive touch and interaction — rather than in its consumer wearables business.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Tactile sensing for humanoid/dexterous robot hands is drawing real component demand now — a supply-chain niche to map ahead of the robotics capex wave.
insights.quote: We see particularly strong momentum in drones and robotics, especially in dexterous hand tactile sensing.
insights.locator: What application areas are your strongest?

insights.claim: Upbeat's drone controller boards are gaining meaningful traction, indicating the company is selling board-level products and not only chips or sensors.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Board-level products imply higher revenue per unit but lower gross margin than silicon — relevant to how the company's financial profile should be modeled.
insights.locator: At the same time, our drone controller boards

insights.claim: Bone-conduction and contact vibration microphones capture signals that traditional microphones miss and enable clearer signal capture in noisy environments, targeting smart glasses, hearables, voice recorders and AI wearables.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Noise-robust voice pickup is the enabling component for always-listening smart glasses — a bill-of-materials line likely to grow with that form factor.
insights.locator: In consumer electronics, we support a range of devices

insights.claim: On the industrial side, combining vibration sensing with edge AI targets predictive maintenance, equipment monitoring, anomaly detection and condition-based monitoring, with additional growing interest from healthcare devices and broader AIoT.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Industrial predictive maintenance is a higher-margin, stickier end market than consumer wearables — a diversification path worth tracking in revenue mix.

insights.claim: Upbeat Technology was founded in Taiwan and has raised more than USD $20 million in funding since 2021, shipping ultra-low-power RISC-V SoCs and MEMS bone-conduction microphones that entered Tier 1 brands in the US and Japan by 2023.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: A modestly funded Taiwanese startup already inside Tier 1 US/Japan supply chains — a credible acquisition target for larger sensor or MCU vendors.
insights.locator: Subsequently, he returned to Taiwan to establish Upbeat Technology

insights.claim: Founder Jerry Chen's background spans IC design at Intel, Lucent, Apple and Procket Network from 1995, then marketing leadership at Inphi/Marvell and Genesys Logic, where in 2011 he led image-processing IC designs into Tier 1 brands including Google at monthly shipments exceeding one million units.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Prior million-unit-per-month Tier 1 ramp experience is the credibility signal that separates edge-AI startups that can scale from those that cannot.
insights.locator: In 2011, he served as BU Head at Genesys Logic

insights.claim: Upbeat's stated founding year in the interview is 2017, which sits alongside a bio noting funding raised only since 2021 — implying a roughly four-year self-funded or pre-institutional development period before the current capital base.
insights.speaker: Jerry Chen
insights.so_what: Long pre-funding gestation is typical of MEMS/silicon hardware startups and lengthens the expected time-to-scale versus software-based AI startups.
